questions.question: State the PPC's assumptions, and explain what points on, inside and beyond the curve each mean.
questions.expected_answer: Assumptions: only two goods; fixed quantity and quality of resources; fixed technology; full and efficient employment. On the curve: efficient and attainable — every point a maximum, with the choice among them being society's (the WHAT question). Inside: attainable but inefficient — idle or misused resources; where unemployment and recession live. Beyond: unattainable with current resources and technology — reachable only if the curve itself shifts.

questions.question: Use the maize-vegetables schedule to show increasing opportunity cost and explain why the curve bows outward.
questions.expected_answer: Successive 10-tonne gains in maize cost 5, 7, 10, 13 and 15 tonnes of vegetables — the opportunity cost of maize rises as more is produced. The cause: resources are not equally suited to all uses — the first fields and hands switched are those best for maize; pushing further converts resources that grew vegetables brilliantly and grow maize poorly, so each extra tonne costs more than the last. A straight-line PPC would claim perfectly interchangeable resources; the outward bow tells the truer story.

questions.question: Distinguish movements along, toward and of the curve; sort the curve's movers into internal and external factors; and trace the consequences of producing inside the curve.
questions.expected_answer: Along the curve: reallocation between goods, same capacity. From inside toward the curve: recovery — employing idle resources, the cheapest growth. The curve shifting outward: growth in capacity itself (inward: capacity lost). Internal movers: more/better resources, capital accumulation, education, technology, efficiency. External: weather, world markets and prices, imported technology, shocks and disasters. Inside-the-curve consequences chain: lost output → lost incomes → lost spending → lost tax revenue, with skills decaying and capacity eroding so tomorrow's curve pulls inward — South Africa's unemployment as the visible gap. Policy order: reach the curve, then move it.
